questions: how to monitor multicast with snmp
what is the ip multicast mib
subtitle: A protocol-independent set of SNMP objects for watching and configuring IP multicast on routers and hosts.

tldr.problem: Operators need a standard way to manage multicast, including its routing, no matter which multicast routing protocol a device runs. The earlier MIB, RFC 2932, handled only IPv4 routing with one protocol per interface.
tldr.mechanism: The IPMCAST-MIB module defines two scalars and eight tables covering interfaces, Source-Specific Multicast ranges, routes, next hops, scope boundaries, scope names, local listeners and scope zones. It supports IPv4 and IPv6.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 2932 and lets hosts as well as routers be managed. Its writeable objects and its readable objects both carry security risks that must be protected, for example with SNMPv3.

today: RFC 5132 is a Proposed Standard that obsoleted RFC 2932. The metadata for this RFC lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the IP Multicast MIB Covers
sections.content:
This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for managing IP multicast function, including IP multicast routing. The objects are independent of the specific multicast routing protocol in use. Objects specific to a particular multicast protocol are defined elsewhere.

Managed objects are reached through a virtual information store, usually with the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP). Objects are defined with the Structure of Management Information, and this module complies with SMIv2 (STD 58: RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580).

The module is named IPMCAST-MIB. Its identity sits at { mib-2 168 }, a number IANA assigned for it. It uses textual conventions from the IF-MIB, the INET-ADDRESS-MIB and the IANA-RTPROTO-MIB.
sections.eli5: This is a standard list of dials and counters for watching multicast traffic on a network device. It works the same whatever protocol the device uses.

sections.title: How It Differs from RFC 2932
sections.content:
This document obsoletes RFC 2932. The new module is a re-working of the old one, with these changes:

  • It supports IPv6 addressing and the IPv6 scoped address architecture. RFC 2932 supported only IPv4.
  • Several multicast protocols can route on one interface. RFC 2932 assumed at most one per interface, so the protocol is now recorded per route, in ipMcastRouteProtocol.
  • It includes objects not specific to routing, so systems that do not route can be managed. RFC 2932 was restricted to multicast routing.
  • It adds a table of Source-Specific Multicast (SSM) address ranges, a table of local applications receiving multicast data, and a table of multicast scope zones.
sections.eli5: An older dashboard only worked for one kind of address and one kind of router rule per connection. The new one handles both address kinds, lets many rules share a connection, and also works for plain computers.

sections.title: The Eight Tables
sections.content:
The module holds two scalars and eight tables. The scalar ipMcastEnabled shows or sets whether IP multicast function is enabled on the system, and ipMcastRouteEntryCount counts rows in the route table so that routing activity and table size can be monitored.

The tables are:

  • Interface table: multicast information specific to interfaces.
  • SSM range table: one row per range of group addresses to which Source-Specific Multicast semantics should be applied.
  • Route table: routing information for datagrams sent by particular sources to the multicast groups the system knows.
  • Route next hop table: the next hops on outgoing interfaces for each source and group.
  • Scope boundary table: the boundaries configured for administratively scoped multicast.
  • Scope name table: human-readable names for multicast scopes.
  • Local listener table: identifiers for local applications that are receiving multicast data.
  • Zone table: one entry per scope zone known to the system, mapping each zone to the multicast address range of its scope.

Several tables are indexed by an address, a prefix length and an address type, so one row can cover a range of groups or sources. Address bits beyond the prefix length are set to zero, because any non-zero bit would name a different row.
sections.eli5: The dashboard is split into eight pages: one for each connection, one for special shows, one for routes, one for next stops, one for fences, one for fence names, one for who is listening, and one for zones.

sections.title: Routes, Next Hops and Counters
sections.content:
Each row in the route table describes datagrams from a source (or all sources) to a group. It records the upstream neighbor, the incoming interface (ipMcastRouteInIfIndex), when the route was learned, how long until it ages out, and the multicast protocol that learned it. An incoming interface of 0 means datagrams are not subject to an incoming interface check and may arrive on several interfaces, for example in BIDIR-PIM.

The route table also holds counters: octets and packets forwarded, octets and packets dropped because the TTL (IPv4) or Hop Limit (IPv6) reached zero or fell below ipMcastInterfaceTtl, and octets and packets dropped because they arrived on an unexpected interface. For protocols such as PIM-SM, that last case is a failed RPF check, where RPF means Reverse Path Forwarding. ipMcastRouteBps reports bits per second as a sample of the last whole 1 second period.

The next hop table lists the outgoing interfaces and next-hop addresses for each source and group. Its state is either pruned(1) or forwarding(2). A pruned entry reverts to forwarding when the prune timer expires. Each next hop also has octet and packet counters.

The interface table has two writeable settings per IP version and interface: ipMcastInterfaceTtl, a threshold from 0 to 256 below which datagrams are not forwarded out the interface (default 0 forwards everything, 256 forwards nothing), and ipMcastInterfaceRateLimit, in kilobits per second, where 0 means no limit.
sections.eli5: For every show being passed along, the router keeps a card: where it came from, where it goes next, and how much has gone through. It also counts the pieces it threw away and why.

sections.title: SSM Ranges, Scopes and Zones
sections.content:
The SSM range table is where an administrator lists group address ranges that should get Source-Specific Multicast semantics. For IPv6, only ranges prefixed by FF3x::/16 are permitted, where x is a valid IPv6 multicast scope. If non-global SSM ranges are present, matching boundary entries are required on the routers at the zone boundary.

The scope boundary table lists the multicast scope boundaries configured on each interface, with counters of multicast octets and packets dropped because of the boundary. Scoped IPv4 ranges must be prefixed by 239.0.0.0/8. Scoped IPv6 ranges are FF0x::/16, and a boundary for FF0x implies the same boundary for the FF1x and FF3x prefixes, so those get no separate rows.

The scope name table gives each scope a name per language tag, suitable for showing to end users. If no name is set, the default for IPv4 is a string like 239.x.x.x/y and for IPv6 it is FF0x::/16. The zone table maps each zone index to its scope address range and records the default zone for that scope. Zone index 0 is not a valid row index.

The local listener table lists applications and services on the device that have joined multicast groups. Each row carries a run index that identifies the software; a value of 0 means one or more unidentified applications have joined.
sections.eli5: Administrators can mark special groups, put fences around areas so that shows do not leak out, and give each area a friendly name like Office instead of a number.

sections.title: Compliance for Hosts and Routers
sections.content:
The MIB ends with conformance information that defines two compliance statements: one for hosts and one for routers. Both say that support for either IPv4 or IPv6 is mandatory, support for both is optional, and support for the zoned address types is optional.

For hosts, the basic group and the local listener group are mandatory. The SSM, route, route diagnostics, boundary and scope name groups are optional. Write access to ipMcastEnabled and to the device storage type is not required for hosts.

The router statement additionally makes the route protocol group mandatory and treats the diagnostics, boundary and scope name groups as optional. Most objects also carry a storage type, so an agent can say whether a row survives a restart, and many rows can be created or removed with a row status object.
sections.eli5: Plain computers only have to fill in the basic pages. Routers have to fill in the routing pages too.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Many objects in this MIB have a MAX-ACCESS of read-write or read-create, and the RFC lists them. Using SET operations without proper protection can hurt network operations. The RFC names two kinds of harm:

  • Changes to multicast routing that break or disrupt services, including delivery of multicast data.
  • Changes that allow interception or subversion of information, for example passing chosen multicast streams through a chosen location without the sources or listeners noticing.

Readable objects can also be sensitive. Reading them can reveal the topology, disposition and composition of the network, and whether multicast data is flowing, plus the locations of senders and recipients. The RFC warns that an attacker can apply traffic analysis to this and that the result can be as damaging as full knowledge of the data. It stresses controlling even GET and NOTIFY access, and possibly encrypting values sent over SNMP. It is RECOMMENDED to use the SNMPv3 security features, and deploying SNMP versions before SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: The dials can be used to cause trouble, and the gauges can show an outsider who is watching what. So only trusted people should be allowed to turn or read them.
